tier_reason: arXiv 2502.05613 (Sec. 5.4, Fig. 5, Table 1) benchmarks ConsensusRecSplit against RecSplit and others. The code is public in ByteHamster/MPHF-Experiments (src/comparison.cpp, contenders/recsplit/ConsensusContender.cpp, contenders/recsplit/RecSplitContender.cpp), and the paper states GNU C++ 11.2.0, -O3 -march=native and an Intel i7-11700.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Against RecSplit (paper Table 1, 100M random string keys, single-threaded): RecSplit l=12,b=2000 reaches 1.613 bits/key at 25,667 ns/key construction. ConsensusRecSplit k=256,eps=0.1 reaches 1.578 bits/key at 248 ns/key, about 103x faster construction at lower space (derived from page data). ConsensusRecSplit k=32768,eps=0.0005 reaches 1.444 bits/key at 30,245 ns/key, roughly the same time RecSplit needs for 1.613 bits/key. The paper's '>350x faster at 1.489 bits/key' is against bipartite ShockHash-RS (the previous most space-efficient approach), not RecSplit. The project README separately states that on 100M keys, with about an hour of construction, it reaches 1.4448 bits/key (lower bound 1.4427) where RecSplit reaches 1.6127 bits/key.
corrections.workload: Single-threaded construction of MPHFs over 100 million random string keys (uniform random length 10-50), plotting space overhead (bits/key) against construction throughput for ConsensusRecSplit versus RecSplit, SIMDRecSplit, ShockHash-RS and bipartite ShockHash-RS/-Flat.
corrections.caveats: The comparison is by the ConsensusRecSplit authors (their MPHF-Experiments framework), single-threaded, on 100M string keys. The headline '>350x' figure is against bipartite ShockHash-RS, not RecSplit. Queries are not faster: 140-217 ns vs RecSplit's 139-156 ns in Table 1. The paper includes only approaches below 1.6 bits/key, so it has no BBHash/CMPH/PTHash comparison. The latest GitHub release (tag 2026-01-04) points at the 2025-06-23 commit.

notes: The claim credited the '>350x at 1.489 bits/key' result to RecSplit, but both arXiv v1 and v2 say it is against bipartite ShockHash-RS; against RecSplit the page supports about 100x at lower space. The 1.4448/1.6127 figures come from the repo README, not the arXiv page (the paper's Table 1 gives 1.444/1.613). The last commit is 2025-06-23 (the 2026-01-04 date is a release tag on that same commit), so the repo is stale, not active.

tier_reason: roberto-trani/mphf_benchmark (src/mphf_benchmark.cpp, include/emphf_wrapper.hpp, include/chd_wrapper.hpp linking libcmph from the bonitao/cmph submodule) runs emphf against CMPH's CHD. The README states the i9-9900K CPU, CMakeLists.txt sets -O3 -march=native, and the PTHash SIGIR'21 paper, whose Table 5 the README reproduces, states gcc 9.2.1.

corrections.claimed_speedup: On mphf_benchmark (PTHash SIGIR'21 Table 5, 1 billion random 64-bit keys, single core, i9-9900K), emphf builds in 374 s at 2.61 bits/key. CMPH's CHD needs 1972 / 5964 / 23746 s for lambda=4/5/6 (2.17/2.07/2.01 bits/key), so emphf builds about 5.3-63x faster (derived from page data). emphf lookups take 199 ns/key vs CHD's 416-419 ns/key, about 2.1x faster (derived from page data), but emphf uses 0.4-0.6 more bits/key. Separately, the rchikhi/benchmphf README reports emphf's HEM variant building a 1-billion-key MPHF in 770 s using 24 GB, vs the 'phf' library's 3900 s and 48 GB, about 5x faster (derived from page data); that page gives no CMPH numbers.
corrections.workload: Single-core construction and lookup of MPHFs over 1 billion random 64-bit keys, comparing emphf (in-memory seq peeling) against CMPH's CHD algorithm (mphf_benchmark table). Separately compared against the 'phf' library in rchikhi/benchmphf's own 1-billion-key test.
corrections.caveats: The benchmark is the PTHash authors' harness, not emphf's own. emphf builds and looks up faster than CMPH's CHD but uses more space (2.61 vs 2.01-2.17 bits/key). On the same table it is slower than BBHash gamma=1 (253 s build, 170 ns lookup) and much slower at lookup than PTHash. emphf's README makes no CMPH-specific claim; it only calls compute_mphf_seq 'the fastest MPHF construction implementation that we know of' (2013). GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is the Apache-2.0 notice. There have been no commits since 2013-12-06.

notes: Numbers match the EMPHF and CHD rows of the mphf_benchmark README; the ratios are now marked as derived. last_commit was the repo's pushed_at date (2024-05-29); the only branch's last commit is 2013-12-06, so the repo is abandoned. The license was checked in the LICENSE file (Apache-2.0).

tier_reason: roberto-trani/mphf_benchmark (src/mphf_benchmark.cpp, include/pthash_wrapper.hpp, include/bbhash_wrapper.hpp with the rizkg/BBHash submodule) runs PTHash against BBHash. The README states the i9-9900K CPU, CMakeLists.txt sets -O3 -march=native, and the PTHash SIGIR'21 paper (Sec. 5) states gcc 9.2.1 and single-core runs.

corrections.claimed_speedup: At similar space (~3 bits/key) on 1 billion random 64-bit keys, single core, PTHash lookups take 37 ns/key (C-C, alpha=0.99, c=7, 3.23 bits/key) and 55 ns/key (D-D, alpha=0.94, c=7, 2.99 bits/key), vs 170 ns/key for BBHash gamma=1 (3.06 bits/key). That is about 3.1-4.6x faster lookups (derived from page data); the paper text says 3-4.5x vs BBHash gamma=1,2. BBHash builds faster at that setting (253 s vs 689-1042 s for these PTHash variants).
corrections.workload: Construction and lookup of MPHFs over 1 billion uniformly random 64-bit integer keys, single core (construction and lookup single-threaded; BBHash also run with one thread), reproducing Table 5 of the PTHash SIGIR'21 paper.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.2.1, -O3 -march=native (PTHash SIGIR'21 paper Sec. 5; mphf_benchmark CMakeLists.txt sets -O3 -march=native)
corrections.caveats: The benchmark is by the PTHash authors, and the README table reproduces their own SIGIR'21 Table 5. That table includes GOV, which is Java-only and cannot be run by the harness. The README lists D-D alpha=0.88 with c=7, but the paper and code use c=11. BBHash was run single-threaded even though it supports multi-threaded construction, and PTHash builds slower than BBHash at similar space. CMPH's CHD was benchmarked directly via libcmph; only CMPH's FCH was replaced by the authors' own FCH reimplementation, because CMPH's FCH was 'orders of magnitude slower'.

notes: Numbers match the PTHash and BBHash rows of the mphf_benchmark README; the ratio is now marked as derived. The '8-thread construction' in the workload came from the PTHash repo's own benchmarks README (Xeon W-2245, gcc 10.3.0), not from this table, which was run on a single core. The old caveat wrongly said CMPH was not benchmarked directly. The metadata (MIT, 267 stars, last commit 2026-07-27, active) checks out.
